document.title: Fast Pseudorandom Correlation Functions from Sparse LPN

candidate.title: A Subexponential-Query PCF from Sparse LPN
candidate.subtitle: Subexponential in queries as well as in runtime, from sparse LPN, in the random oracle model
candidate.one_line: Some pseudorandom correlation function based on sparse LPN is secure against an adversary that runs for subexponential time and asks for subexponentially many correlations, not merely superpolynomially many.
candidate.informal: A pseudorandom correlation function turns a pair of short keys into as much correlated randomness as two parties will ever need, with no further interaction. The source paper gives the first construction that is both fast and based on a well-studied assumption, sparse LPN, and pays for it in the asymptotics: its security survives a subexponential-time adversary only while that adversary asks for at most superpolynomially many correlations, where earlier candidates from newer assumptions plausibly tolerated subexponentially many. The conjecture is that the gap is an artefact of the construction rather than of the assumption.
candidate.status_note: Open in both directions. The source poses it as the first of its two open questions and takes no position; the affirmative direction stated here is the page's own reading. The source's own construction is secure against subexponential-time adversaries for up to n^(log n / log log n) queries.
candidate.progress_note: No partial result towards it is reported. The source names the shortfall but no obstruction. The one follow-up construction from sparse LPN, ePrint 2025/2002, inherits the same superpolynomial ceiling and says so.

quotes.text: Is it possible to build a PCF with fully-subexponential security (in runtime and queries) from sparse LPN?
Our PCF only achieves subexponential security up to superpolynomially-many queries, a lower asymptotic security level compared to previous candidates.
Open Questions. We mention two interesting open questions:

Compared with previous constructions from VDLPN, EALPN, DCR, or QR, our PCF comes with a theoretical limitation: while previous constructions were plausibly secure against a (subexponential-time) adversary requesting a subexponential number of PCF evaluations,
these parameters achieve security with inverse-superpolynomial advantage against subexponential-time adversaries making at most superpolynomially-many queries to the PCF
evaluation must run in polynomial time

candidate.why_interesting: It is the one respect in which moving PCFs onto a well-established assumption made the asymptotic security worse, and the source's construction is otherwise the state of the art. Settling it either closes that gap or shows the recursion is inherent.
candidate.why_clean: The PCF security notion is quantitative in the source's own Definition 9, with explicit N, B and epsilon, so 'subexponential in runtime and queries' has a formal home; and the correlation and assumption are both the source's.
candidate.risks: The source names no obstruction at all, which is the weakest point: the page supplies the parameter tension (evaluation cost k^L against stretch m^(L)) from the source's printed constraints rather than from any claim the source makes about difficulty. Also check the two readings recorded in the second remark: whether the advantage should be subexponentially small (the source's phrase constrains only runtime and queries) and whether the sparsity should be pinned to polylog(n).
candidate.formal_statement_latex: There exist a constant $\delta > 0$, a field $\F_{p^{r}}$, parameter functions $n(\lambda) = \poly(\lambda)$, $m(\lambda)$, $t(\lambda)$ and $k(\lambda)$ with $3 \le k(\lambda) \le n(\lambda)$, and a pair of algorithms $(\Gen, \Eval)$ with keys of size $\poly(\lambda)$, such that $(\Gen, \Eval)$ is an $(N, B, \varepsilon)$-secure strong PCF for the subfield VOLE correlation over $\F_{p^{r}}$ with $N(\lambda) = B(\lambda) = 2^{\lambda^{\delta}}$ and $\varepsilon(\lambda) = 2^{-\lambda^{\delta}}$, assuming only that $\SparseLPN(k, n, m, \Reg_{t}, \F_{p})$ is $(2^{\lambda^{\delta'}}, 2^{-\lambda^{\delta'}})$-hard for some constant $\delta' > 0$, together with a random oracle.

verify.reason: The question is printed verbatim in a section titled 'Open Questions' on p. 10 and is not answered anywhere in the paper, whose last section is 4.5 and which contains no theorem about query bounds beyond Theorem 1's a-priori-fixed ones. Two corrections were forced on the first draft: it pinned the sparsity to polylog(n), which strengthens the statement beyond the question asked, and it left the advantage requirement unflagged where the source's phrase constrains only runtime and queries.

checks.name: existence
checks.finding: Printed verbatim under 'Open Questions. We mention two interesting open questions:' as item (1).

checks.name: openness
checks.finding: The paper's last section is 4.5 (pp. 30-32), there is no conclusion after it, and no lemma, claim or theorem addresses the query regime beyond Theorem 1, whose bounds QA, QB, QO are fixed a priori. Checked the full list of numbered results (Theorem 1, Lemmas 2-6, Claims 1-2, Definitions 1-10).

checks.name: strength
checks.finding: The first draft required k = polylog(n), which the question does not: Definition 5 allows any k in [3, n], and the polylog choice belongs to the source's conservative flavour of the assumption (Section 1.4, p. 6). Corrected.

checks.name: quantifiers-and-parameters
checks.finding: 'Fully-subexponential security (in runtime and queries)' does not say what the advantage must be, and the source's own result has inverse-superpolynomial advantage (p. 16). The statement asks for one exponent to serve size, queries and advantage, and the remark now records the weaker reading explicitly.

checks.name: attribution
checks.finding: The source's own open question about its own construction, not a question it attributes to anyone else.

checks.name: definitions
checks.finding: PCF is the source's Definition 9 (after Boyle et al.), sparse LPN its Definition 5 (p. 11), subfield VOLE its Definition 10 (p. 13). All three are reproduced from the source rather than replaced by standard variants.

checks.name: fabrication
checks.finding: The first draft quoted the parameter constraint as 'we require k L = poly(n)', which is the text layer's rendering of $k^L$; that would print a typo on the page as if it were the source's. Replaced by the prose fragment 'evaluation must run in polynomial time' plus the exponent set in mathematics.

checks.name: self-containment
checks.finding: The statement is readable from the page's own Definitions 5 and 9 and the notation list; no symbol is used undefined and no defined symbol is unused.

corrections.problem: Pinned the sparsity to polylog(n), strengthening the statement past the question asked.
corrections.corrected: Quantify k only over Definition 5's range 3 <= k <= n, and record the polylog reading in a remark.

corrections.problem: Quoted 'we require k L = poly(n)', a text-layer artefact for $k^L$.
corrections.corrected: Quote only 'evaluation must run in polynomial time' and set the exponent in mathematics.

corrections.problem: The advantage requirement was stated without flagging that the source's phrase does not constrain it.
corrections.corrected: Added the second remark naming both readings, and the weaker one the statement implies.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: The conjecture that a high dual distance is all that is needed for a sparse LPN instance to be as secure as standard LPN (Section 4.2, p. 23).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: Not the source's own conjecture -- it attributes it to ADINZ17 and BCM25 -- and the source says it is not formalizable as stated: 'Note that the conjecture is not fully formal: there are known counter-examples (typically, Reed-Solomon codes)'. A page would have to invent the formalization the literature has not settled.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: The binary-SVP-style assumption that low-weight kernel vectors are hard to find even when they exist (Section 4.2, p. 24).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: The source calls it a 'very reasonable assumption' that was 'explicitly required and studied in multiple works', i.e. an assumption the parameter selection makes, not an open problem this paper poses. prompts/harvest.md rejects security assumptions dressed as conjectures by name.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: Whether the sparse-product noise distribution used for the stateless variant affects security (Section 1.5, p. 10).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: The source says only that it 'does not appear to have any impact on security' while cautioning that a new construction warrants care. That is a hedge about its own optimization, with no proposition attached and no claim that anything is open.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: Extending the concrete dual-distance computation to general fields at the dimensions the construction uses (Section 4.5, p. 32).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: An engineering and algorithmic-cost problem -- the formulae exist and are at least cubic in n -- rather than a mathematical claim to prove or refute. It is recorded as the obstruction on the page for the field-size conjecture instead.
